claim: The medial olfactory tubercle (mOT) is involved in both reward and olfaction.
source: The medial olfactory tubercle (mOT) is involved in both reward and olfaction, whereas the ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic (DAergic) neurons are considered to be engaged in reward and motivation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information.

claim: The VTA dopaminergic neurons are engaged in reward and motivation.
source: The medial olfactory tubercle (mOT) is involved in both reward and olfaction, whereas the ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic (DAergic) neurons are considered to be engaged in reward and motivation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information.

claim: The VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can be activated by different types of naturalistic rewards in DAT-cre mice.
source: Here, we found that the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway could be activated by different types of naturalistic rewards as well as odors in DAT-cre mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data showing activation in response to sucrose, food pellets, and social interaction (Figure 2).

claim: The VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can be activated by odors in DAT-cre mice.
source: Here, we found that the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway could be activated by different types of naturalistic rewards as well as odors in DAT-cre mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry recordings showing mOT neuron responses to various odors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers elicits preference for space.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers was able to elicit preferences for space, location and neutral odor, while pharmacological blockade of the dopamine receptors in the mOT fully prevented the odor-preference formation.
evidence: This is supported by RTPP and iClass behavioral experiments (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers elicits preference for location.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers was able to elicit preferences for space, location and neutral odor, while pharmacological blockade of the dopamine receptors in the mOT fully prevented the odor-preference formation.
evidence: This is supported by RTPP and iClass behavioral experiments (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers elicits preference for neutral odor.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers was able to elicit preferences for space, location and neutral odor, while pharmacological blockade of the dopamine receptors in the mOT fully prevented the odor-preference formation.
evidence: This is supported by odor-light pairing experiments (Figure 5C).

claim: Pharmacological blockade of the dopamine receptors in the mOT fully prevented odor-preference formation.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic fibers was able to elicit preferences for space, location and neutral odor, while pharmacological blockade of the dopamine receptors in the mOT fully prevented the odor-preference formation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using D1R and D2R antagonists (Figure 5F).

claim: Inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons eliminated the previously formed odor-preference.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons eliminated the previously formed odor-preference and strongly affected the Go-no go learning efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic inactivation experiments (Figure 7G).

claim: Inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons strongly affected the Go-no go learning efficiency.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons eliminated the previously formed odor-preference and strongly affected the Go-no go learning efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by Go-no go task experiments with chemogenetic inactivation (Figure 7H).

claim: The VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway mediates a variety of naturalistic reward processes.
source: In summary, our results revealed that the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway mediates a variety of naturalistic reward processes and different types of preferences including odor-preference in mice.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experiments showing activation by rewards and behavioral effects.

claim: The VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway mediates different types of preferences including odor-preference in mice.
source: In summary, our results revealed that the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway mediates a variety of naturalistic reward processes and different types of preferences including odor-preference in mice.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple behavioral experiments.

claim: Reward-related odor perception is critical for food foraging and reproduction in rodents.
source: For rodents, reward-related odor perception is critical for food foraging and reproduction (Doty, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The olfactory tubercle (OT) is a long and narrow tubular brain structure located at the ventral part of striatum.
source: The olfactory tubercle (OT) is a long and narrow tubular brain structure located at the ventral part of striatum.
evidence: This is an anatomical description based on established knowledge.

claim: The OT belongs to the olfactory system and receives dense direct inputs from the main olfactory bulb (OB).
source: It belongs to the olfactory system and receives dense direct inputs from the main olfactory bulb (OB) and other olfactory cortexes such as the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON) and piriform cortex (PCX) (Wesson and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT receives dense direct inputs from the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON).
source: It belongs to the olfactory system and receives dense direct inputs from the main olfactory bulb (OB) and other olfactory cortexes such as the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON) and piriform cortex (PCX) (Wesson and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT receives dense direct inputs from the piriform cortex (PCX).
source: It belongs to the olfactory system and receives dense direct inputs from the main olfactory bulb (OB) and other olfactory cortexes such as the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON) and piriform cortex (PCX) (Wesson and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT belongs to both the olfactory and reward circuits.
source: Belonging to both the olfactory and reward circuits (Ikemoto, 2007; Wesson and Wilson, 2011), the OT is at the proper position to play critical roles in the formation of odor-preference.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The OT encodes natural reinforcers.
source: The OT encodes natural reinforcers (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016), odor valence and pheromone reward (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016; DiBenedictis et al., 2015; Agustín-Pavón et al., 2014), and also influences reward behaviors and odor-preferences (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT encodes odor valence.
source: The OT encodes natural reinforcers (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016), odor valence and pheromone reward (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016; DiBenedictis et al., 2015; Agustín-Pavón et al., 2014), and also influences reward behaviors and odor-preferences (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The OT encodes pheromone reward.
source: The OT encodes natural reinforcers (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016), odor valence and pheromone reward (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016; DiBenedictis et al., 2015; Agustín-Pavón et al., 2014), and also influences reward behaviors and odor-preferences (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The OT influences reward behaviors and odor-preferences.
source: The OT encodes natural reinforcers (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016), odor valence and pheromone reward (Gadziola and Wesson, 2016; DiBenedictis et al., 2015; Agustín-Pavón et al., 2014), and also influences reward behaviors and odor-preferences (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific domains of the OT represent reward or punishment-associated odor-cues.
source: Furthermore, specific domains of the OT represent reward or punishment-associated odor-cues (Murata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The VTA can modulate the activities of olfactory-related OT neurons.
source: An earlier study showed that the VTA can modulate the activities of olfactory-related OT neurons (Mooney et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The VTA DAergic neurons play central roles in general reward and motivation via innervating the ventral striatum.
source: The VTA DAergic neurons have been proposed to play central roles in general reward and motivation, via innervating the ventral striatum (Hu, 2016; Roeper, 2013; Ungless et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most of the OT neurons are D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons.
source: As a component of the ventral striatum, most of the OT neurons are D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (Murata et al., 2015; Millhouse and Heimer, 1984), which are heavily innervated by DAergic neurons from the VTA (Voorn et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The medial OT (mOT) is more involved in addiction, reward and reward associated odor perceptions compared with the lateral OT.
source: Compared with the lateral OT, the medial OT (mOT) is more involved in addiction, reward and reward associated odor perceptions (Murata et al., 2015; Ikemoto, 2005; Ikemoto, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mOT mediates self-administration of cocaine or D-amphetamine even more robustly than the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
source: In fact, the mOT mediates self-administration of cocaine or D-amphetamine even more robustly than the nucleus accumbens (NAc), which is crucially important for reward learning and drug abuse (Koob and Volkow, 2010; Ikemoto, 2005, 2003; Rodd-Henricks et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RV-labeled neurons were widely distributed in the olfactory systems including the OB and PCX.
source: RV-labeled neurons were widely distributed in the olfactory systems including the OB, PCX (Figure 1C–F), and entorhinal cortex (data not shown), as well as reward related brain regions such as a large area of the VTA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RV tracing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RV-labeled neurons were distributed in the entorhinal cortex.
source: RV-labeled neurons were widely distributed in the olfactory systems including the OB, PCX (Figure 1C–F), and entorhinal cortex (data not shown), as well as reward related brain regions such as a large area of the VTA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: RV-labeled neurons were distributed in reward related brain regions such as a large area of the VTA.
source: RV-labeled neurons were widely distributed in the olfactory systems including the OB, PCX (Figure 1C–F), and entorhinal cortex (data not shown), as well as reward related brain regions such as a large area of the VTA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RV tracing data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In the OB, a large number of neurons in the mitral cell layers were labeled by RV.
source: In the OB, a large number of neurons in the mitral cell layers as well as a small number of neurons in the external plexiform layer were labeled by RV (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by RV tracing data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: In the OB, a small number of neurons in the external plexiform layer were labeled by RV.
source: In the OB, a large number of neurons in the mitral cell layers as well as a small number of neurons in the external plexiform layer were labeled by RV (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by RV tracing data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: RV also labeled many neurons in the hippocampus.
source: Besides, RV also labeled many neurons in other brain regions including the hippocampus and dorsal raphe (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: RV also labeled many neurons in the dorsal raphe.
source: Besides, RV also labeled many neurons in other brain regions including the hippocampus and dorsal raphe (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: About half of the GFP labeled cells (55.32%, n = 3 mice) in the VTA were TH positive.
source: We then examined the cell types of RV infected neurons in the VTA by immunochemical staining of the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), a biomarker of DAergic neurons, and found about half of the GFP labeled cells (55.32%, n = 3 mice) were TH positive (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: When the mice sought and acquired sucrose solution, the GCaMP fluorescence was reliably increased (p<0.001, t-test, n = 6).
source: When the mice sought and acquired sucrose solution, the GCaMP fluorescence was reliably increased (p<0.001, t-test, n = 6, Figure 2B–D-left).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The GCaMP signals were reliably increased with food pellet consumption (p<0.001, t-test, n = 5).
source: We then tested the solid food intake and found that the GCaMP signals were also reliably increased with food pellet consumption (p<0.001, t-test, n = 5, Figure 2D-middle).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2D-middle.

claim: Reliable increases of GCaMP fluorescence were observed during social interaction (p<0.001, t-test, n = 6).
source: We examined the effect of male-female and male-male interactions, and observed reliable increases of GCaMP fluorescence individually. Because no significant difference of fluorescence changes were observed between the male-female and male-male social interactions, we pooled the data of social interaction experiments (p<0.001, t-test, n = 6, Figure 2D-right).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2D-right.

claim: No significant difference of fluorescence changes were observed between the male-female and male-male social interactions.
source: We examined the effect of male-female and male-male interactions, and observed reliable increases of GCaMP fluorescence individually. Because no significant difference of fluorescence changes were observed between the male-female and male-male social interactions, we pooled the data of social interaction experiments (p<0.001, t-test, n = 6, Figure 2D-right).
evidence: This is stated based on statistical analysis of fiber photometry data.

claim: The VTA-mOT DAergic projection showed a higher response to reward stimuli compared with aversive ones.
source: We found that the VTA-mOT DAergic projection showed a higher response to reward stimuli compared with aversive ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data comparing sucrose and quinine responses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mOT neurons were generally activated by different odor stimulations, including isoamyl acetate (ISO), carvone (CAR), citral (CIT), and geraniol (GER).
source: It was found that the mOT neurons were generally activated by different odor stimulations, including isoamyl acetate (ISO), carvone (CAR), citral (CIT), and geraniol (GER), respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: About 94.39% of the mCherry+ neurons in the VTA were also labeled with TH.
source: We found that about 94.39% of the mCherry+ neurons were also labeled with TH (Figure 3C–E), suggesting that the expression of ChR2-mCherry is largely restricted to DAergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: 20 Hz blue light pulses reliably induced action potentials in ChR2-expressing neurons.
source: Whole cell recording of light-evoked activity from ChR2-expressing cells in brain slices from these mice revealed that 20 Hz blue light pulses reliably induced action potentials in ChR2-expressing neurons (Figure 3-fugure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Blue light stimulation of the VTA-mOT DAergic projections increased the c-fos expression levels in the OT (p=0.040, t-test).
source: As expected, the OT showed a robust enhancement of c-fos activation (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C. p=0.040, t-test), suggesting that it was strongly activated by stimulation of this pathway.
evidence: This is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The c-fos expression was significantly increased in the NAc compared to the control mice (p=0.006, t-test).
source: In addition, the c-fos expression was significantly increased in the NAc and PCX compared to the control mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D. p=0.006 for NAc, p=0.006 for PCX, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The c-fos expression was significantly increased in the PCX compared to the control mice (p=0.006, t-test).
source: In addition, the c-fos expression was significantly increased in the NAc and PCX compared to the control mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D. p=0.006 for NAc, p=0.006 for PCX, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mice expressing ChR2 exhibited significant preference for the light-paired chamber (76.55 ± 1.25%, n = 7) in RTPP tests.
source: Real-time place preference (RTPP) tests revealed that mice expressing ChR2 exhibited significant preference for the light-paired chamber (76.55 ± 1.25%, n = 7), compared with the control mice (50.22 ± 5.27%, n = 7) which only expressed mCherry (p=0.001, t-test, Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by RTPP behavioral data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Control mice expressing only mCherry showed 50.22 ± 5.27% preference for the light-paired chamber (n = 7) in RTPP tests.
source: Real-time place preference (RTPP) tests revealed that mice expressing ChR2 exhibited significant preference for the light-paired chamber (76.55 ± 1.25%, n = 7), compared with the control mice (50.22 ± 5.27%, n = 7) which only expressed mCherry (p=0.001, t-test, Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by RTPP behavioral data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Optical activation of mice expressing ChR2-mCherry (n = 7) dramatically increased center exploration in iClass tests.
source: Tests with intra-Cranial light administration in a specific subarea (iClass, Figure 4A) exhibited that optic activation of mice expressing ChR2-mCherry (n = 7) dramatically increased center exploration, represented by the significantly enhanced entry and retention times, immediately after the first day of iClass training using 20 Hz light pulses (Figure 4B–F, p=0.017 for center entry times, p=0.017 for center duration in L1; Videos 1–5, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by iClass behavioral data shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: Mice rapidly overcame their instinctive avoidance for the central area in about 6 min from light activation in L1.
source: We segmented the 15 min training course each day into every 3 min sections and found that mice rapidly overcame their instinctive avoidance for the central area in about 6 min from light activation in L1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by iClass behavioral data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The preference of mice for the light-paired central area increased with light training.
source: The preference of mice for the light-paired central area increased with light training (2.76 ± 1.08, 14.81 ± 4.00, 35.34 ± 6.04 and 52.03 ± 5.27 central entry times; 13.29 ± 5.76%, 42.29 ± 11.49%, 78.86 ± 9.11%, and 85.86 ± 9.79% central retention for Pre, L1, L2 and L3, respectively) and was still maintained 24 hr later when no light pulse was delivered (33.80 ± 4.23 for central entry times, p<0.001; 66.86 ± 5.66% for central retention, p<0.001, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by iClass behavioral data.

claim: The ChR2-expressing mice showed a higher percentage of investigation time to the paired odor (geraniol) compared with the non-paired (carvone) (p=0.012, n = 8, t-test).
source: As shown in Figure 5C, we chose one pair of odors (carvone and geraniol), each of them is equivalently sampled by naive mice and found that the ChR2-expressing mice showed a higher percentage of investigation time to the paired odor (geraniol) compared with the non-paired (carvone) (p=0.012, n = 8, t-test, Video 6) or the control mice (p=0.053, n = 8, t-test), while the two odors still remained equivalently sampled by the control mice after pairing with optical stimulation (p=0.575, n = 8, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by odor-preference test data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After pairing, the ChR2-expressing mice (n = 8) spent a significantly higher percentage of investigation time for TMT, compared with the control mice (p=0.049, n = 8, t-test).
source: As shown in Figure 5D, after pairing, the ChR2-expressing mice (n = 8) spent a significantly higher percentage of investigation time for TMT, compared with the control mice (p=0.049, n = 8, t-test) and unpaired odor (p=0.025, t-test), reaching the level equivalent to sesame butter (p=0.680, n = 8).
evidence: This is supported by odor-preference test data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Administration of D1 and D2 dopamine receptor antagonists abolished the formation of preference for the paired odor (p=0.757, n = 6, t-test).
source: We found that administration of these drugs abolished the formation of preference for the paired odor (Figure 5F, p=0.757, n = 6, t-test), which is preferred by animals with only saline infusion (Figure 5F, p=0.027, n = 6, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by odor-preference test data with receptor antagonists shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The co-labeled rate (1.65%) of the VTA neurons by both GFP and dsRed were negligible.
source: At first, we co-injected RV-dG-GFP into the NAc and RV-dG-dsRed into the mOT (Figure 6A,B) and found that the co-labeled rate (1.65%) of the VTA neurons were negligible, which implied that it may not be common for a VTA DAergic neuron to co-innervate the NAc and the mOT (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by dual RV tracing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most (90.86%) of the mCherry-labeled cells in the VTA were also co-expressing TH.
source: We found that although the mCherry-positive cells only took a small portion (37.20%) of the whole VTA DAergic neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), most (90.86%) of the mCherry-labeled cells were also co-expressing TH (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: The mCherry-positive cells only took a small portion (37.20%) of the whole VTA DAergic neurons.
source: We found that although the mCherry-positive cells only took a small portion (37.20%) of the whole VTA DAergic neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), most (90.86%) of the mCherry-labeled cells were also co-expressing TH (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: After the Go-no go training was performed, inactivating the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons disrupted the conditioned odor-preference.
source: We found that after the Go-no go training was performed, inactivating the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons disrupted the conditioned odor-preference (Figure 7G), but intact odor discrimination remained (Figure 7H, left and middle bar pairs).
evidence: This is supported by Go-no go task data with chemogenetic inactivation shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Inactivating the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons left intact odor discrimination.
source: We found that after the Go-no go training was performed, inactivating the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons disrupted the conditioned odor-preference (Figure 7G), but intact odor discrimination remained (Figure 7H, left and middle bar pairs).
evidence: This is supported by Go-no go task data with chemogenetic inactivation shown in Figure 7H.

claim: When the mOT-projecting VTA neurons were inactivated during the Go-no go training, the learning efficiency of the well-trained mice to a new odor pair was strongly affected (66.17% accuracy vs. 91.00% for control, p=0.002).
source: We further found that when the mOT-projecting VTA neurons were inactivated during the Go-no go training, the learning efficiency of the well-trained mice to a new odor pair was strongly affected (Figure 7H, right bar pair, 66.17% accuracy vs. 91.00% for control, with random level at 50%, p=0.002), suggesting the important roles of the projection to establish the paradigm which can lead to the formation of odor-preference.
evidence: This is supported by Go-no go task data with chemogenetic inactivation shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The control mice showed a significant preference to the S+ odor after the learning session (52.43 ± 5.32% for pre learning, 67.78 ± 3.40% for post learning, p=0.018).
source: The control mice showed a significant preference to the S+ odor after the learning session (Figure 8D, 52.43 ± 5.32% for pre learning, 67.78 ± 3.40% for post learning, p=0.018).
evidence: This is supported by odor-food associative learning data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Optogenetic inhibiting the VTA-mOT DAergic projection during the odor-food associative learning disrupted the conditioned odor-preference of the eNpHR-expressing mice (51.82 ± 2.66% for pre learning, 57.07 ± 3.06% for post learning, p=0.134).
source: However, optogenetic inhibiting the VTA-mOT DAergic projection during the odor-food associative learning disrupted the conditioned odor-preference of the eNpHR-expressing mice (Figure 8D, 51.82 ± 2.66% for pre learning, 57.07 ± 3.06% for post learning, p=0.134).
evidence: This is supported by odor-food associative learning data with optogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Activation of the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can generate preference for a neutral odor or abolish the avoidance for an aversive odor.
source: Then we found that activation of the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can generate preference for a neutral odor or abolish the avoidance for an aversive odor; inhibition of the projection downstream in the mOT through specific dopamine receptor antagonists prevented odor-preference formation completely; and inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons fully blocked the formed odor-preference, and strongly attenuated the Go-no go learning performance which leads to the odor-preference established through naturalistic reward odor-preference.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: Inhibition of the projection downstream in the mOT through specific dopamine receptor antagonists prevented odor-preference formation completely.
source: Then we found that activation of the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can generate preference for a neutral odor or abolish the avoidance for an aversive odor; inhibition of the projection downstream in the mOT through specific dopamine receptor antagonists prevented odor-preference formation completely; and inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons fully blocked the formed odor-preference, and strongly attenuated the Go-no go learning performance which leads to the odor-preference established through naturalistic reward odor-preference.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by receptor antagonist experiments.

claim: Inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons fully blocked the formed odor-preference.
source: Then we found that activation of the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can generate preference for a neutral odor or abolish the avoidance for an aversive odor; inhibition of the projection downstream in the mOT through specific dopamine receptor antagonists prevented odor-preference formation completely; and inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons fully blocked the formed odor-preference, and strongly attenuated the Go-no go learning performance which leads to the odor-preference established through naturalistic reward odor-preference.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by chemogenetic inactivation experiments.

claim: Inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons strongly attenuated the Go-no go learning performance which leads to the odor-preference established through naturalistic reward odor-preference.
source: Then we found that activation of the VTA (DAergic)-mOT pathway can generate preference for a neutral odor or abolish the avoidance for an aversive odor; inhibition of the projection downstream in the mOT through specific dopamine receptor antagonists prevented odor-preference formation completely; and inactivation of the mOT-projecting VTA DAergic neurons fully blocked the formed odor-preference, and strongly attenuated the Go-no go learning performance which leads to the odor-preference established through naturalistic reward odor-preference.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by Go-no go task experiments with chemogenetic inactivation.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the OT promotes reward.
source: Although previous study has shown that electrical stimulation of the OT promotes reward (Fitzgerald et al., 2014), the behavioral effects have never been evaluated by directly targeting the VTA-mOT DAergic projection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ventral striatum is heterogeneously innervated by GABAergic, glutamatergic and DAergic afferents from the VTA.
source: It is reported that the ventral striatum is heterogeneously innervated by GABAergic, glutamatergic and DAergic afferents from the VTA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: DAergic neurons in the VTA are involved in diverse functions, depending on their projection targets.
source: DAergic neurons in the VTA are involved in diverse functions, depending on their projection targets (Kim et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of the trimeric G-protein Gs-coupled D1R increases the excitability of the D1R + neurons.
source: It was reported that activation of the trimeric G-protein Gs-coupled D1R increases the excitability of the D1R + neurons, and that activation of the Gi-coupled D2R decreases the excitability of the D2R + neurons (Stoof and Kebabian, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of the Gi-coupled D2R decreases the excitability of the D2R + neurons.
source: It was reported that activation of the trimeric G-protein Gs-coupled D1R increases the excitability of the D1R + neurons, and that activation of the Gi-coupled D2R decreases the excitability of the D2R + neurons (Stoof and Kebabian, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the OT respond to DAergic terminal activation.
source: Besides, cholinergic neurons in the OT also respond to DAergic terminal activation (Wieland et al., 2014), which might also lead to reward, because rats easily learned to self-administer cholinergic receptor agonists carbachol in the NAc (Ikemoto et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rats easily learned to self-administer cholinergic receptor agonists carbachol in the NAc.
source: Besides, cholinergic neurons in the OT also respond to DAergic terminal activation (Wieland et al., 2014), which might also lead to reward, because rats easily learned to self-administer cholinergic receptor agonists carbachol in the NAc (Ikemoto et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The activities of the VTA DAergic projection are target-dependent in response to rewards and shock.
source: It is reported that the activities of the VTA DAergic projection are target-dependent in response to rewards and shock (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The VTA projection to NAc increases activity during reward and decreases activity during shock.
source: For example, the projection to NAc has been shown to increase activity during reward and decrease activity during shock, while the projection to basolateral-amygdala displayed increased response to both reward and shock.
evidence: This is stated as an example from previous literature.

claim: The VTA projection to basolateral-amygdala displayed increased response to both reward and shock.
source: For example, the projection to NAc has been shown to increase activity during reward and decrease activity during shock, while the projection to basolateral-amygdala displayed increased response to both reward and shock.
evidence: This is stated as an example from previous literature.

claim: The VTA projection to prefrontal cortex exhibited increased activity to shock but not reward.
source: Also, the projection to prefrontal cortex exhibited increased activity to shock but not reward.

claim: The OT neurons encode odor valence by enhancing firing rates.
source: As recent studies have shown that the OT neurons encode odor valence by enhancing firing rates (Gadziola et al., 2015), and that rewarding odor cues preferentially activate the D1R + neurons in the mOT (Murata et al., 2015), the mOT seems to be involved in odor-preference.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rewarding odor cues preferentially activate the D1R + neurons in the mOT.
source: As recent studies have shown that the OT neurons encode odor valence by enhancing firing rates (Gadziola et al., 2015), and that rewarding odor cues preferentially activate the D1R + neurons in the mOT (Murata et al., 2015), the mOT seems to be involved in odor-preference.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The striatum plays an important role in experience-dependent reward learning behaviors.
source: Animals learn to associate diverse sensory cues, not only odors, with rewards depending on their life experience. The striatum plays an important role in experience-dependent reward learning behaviors (Mahon et al., 2004; Wickens et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blockade of the striatum D1R + neurons damages both the visual cue-based reward learning and cocaine-induced conditional place preference.
source: Blockade of the striatum D1R + neurons damages both the visual cue-based reward learning and cocaine-induced conditional place preference (Yawata et al., 2012; Hikida et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activation of striatum D1R is necessary for the generation of corticostriatal LTP that induced by concurrent phasic dopamine release and cortical stimulation.
source: Besides, the activation of striatum D1R is necessary for the generation of corticostriatal LTP that induced by concurrent phasic dopamine release and cortical stimulation (Keeler et al., 2014; Mahon et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The OT neurons respond to an auditory stimulus.
source: As a part of the ventral striatum, the OT neurons also respond to an auditory stimulus (Wesson and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT is composed of the medial and lateral parts, which are functionally different from each other.
source: The OT is composed of the medial and lateral parts, which are functionally different from each other (Murata et al., 2015; DiBenedictis et al., 2015; Agustín-Pavón et al., 2014; Ikemoto, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NAc and OT, components of the ventral striatum, mediate reward processing similarly.
source: Besides, the NAc and OT, components of the ventral striatum, mediate reward processing similarly (Striano et al., 2014; Millhouse and Heimer, 1984) and both are innervated by DAergic projections from the VTA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mOT robustly mediates self-administration of cocaine or D-amphetamine more than the NAc.
source: Previous studies found that the mOT robustly mediates self-administration of cocaine or D-amphetamine more than the NAc (Ikemoto, 2005; Ikemoto, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of DAergic terminals innervating the NAc is sufficient to drive-positive reinforcement.
source: Meanwhile, a recent research reported that optogenetic activation of DAergic terminals innervating the NAc is sufficient to drive-positive reinforcement (Steinberg et al., 2014), whether there would be any functional difference between activation of DAergic projection in the mOT and NAc is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of the VTA-mOT DAergic projection can generate robust rewarding, leading to formation of olfactory as well as spatial preferences if the corresponding stimulation is coupled with the activation of the projection simultaneously.
source: In summary, we have provided evidence that the VTA-mOT DAergic projection can be activated by a variety of rewards and that activation of the projection can generate robust rewarding, leading to formation of olfactory as well as spatial preferences if the corresponding stimulation is coupled with the activation of the projection simultaneously.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results.
